question:
Patient note:
An 86-year-old man who lives alone in a one-story bungalow and still insists on mowing his own lawn was brought to the medical intensive care intake area by advanced life-support ambulance after a neighbor noticed him sitting on his porch looking pale and slightly breathless late this afternoon; according to the neighbor he had complained earlier of a “touch of the flu,” took two acetaminophen tablets, and lay down but received no prescription medications, inhalers, intravenous fluids, or supplemental oxygen until the paramedics arrived. His past history, obtained from a well-kept wallet card and verified by electronic chart review, lists treated hypertension and cataract extraction only; he has never required organ transplantation, dialysis, chemotherapy, chronic corticosteroids, or biologic agents and has no record of cirrhosis, chronic lung disease, advanced heart failure, or immunodeficiency. Paramedics found him seated upright, conversant though mildly confused about the exact date, with an initial automated blood pressure of 142/82 mm Hg that was reproduced on a second cuff; pulse oximetry on ambient air showed 90 %, so they placed a simple face mask attached to the truck blender delivering 38 % inspired oxygen, started one peripheral line without running fluids, and gave no bronchodilators, diuretics, antibiotics, analgesics, or vasopressors during the eight-minute transport. On arrival to the resuscitation bay—and before any emergency department intervention—the first complete set of vitals was captured: oral temperature 98.5 °F, non-invasive blood pressure 140/80 mm Hg confirmed with the manual sphygmomanometer, regular pulse 95 beats per minute displayed on telemetry, and a visually counted respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute without accessory-muscle use. The patient opened his eyes to voice, answered most orientation questions but stumbled on the month, and obeyed two-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 14 in the absence of ethanol or sedatives. Skin was warm and dry with brisk capillary refill; no mottling or peripheral cyanosis was present. Neck veins were not distended at 30°, cardiac auscultation revealed a crisp S1, single physiologic S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and distal pulses were 2+ and symmetric. Breath sounds were vesicular throughout with a few scattered end-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases; percussion remained resonant and there was no wheeze. The abdomen was soft, nondistended, and nontender with active bowel sounds, and there was no flank costovertebral angle pain. Extremities showed no edema, clubbing, or tenderness, and a brief neurologic screen demonstrated equal pupils, symmetric strength, and intact coordination when he touched his nose. A right radial arterial specimen drawn nine minutes after stretcher placement—while the face mask continued to deliver the same 38 % oxygen—yielded a pH of 7.43, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 79 mm Hg; end-tidal CO₂ on waveform capnography was 34 mm Hg. Point-of-care basic metabolic panel returned sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, glucose 118 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 21 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, the last value matching his outpatient baseline recorded at a primary-care visit two months earlier. A complete blood count drawn from the same stick showed white blood cells 12 800 /mm³ with 80 % segmented neutrophils, hematocrit 34 %, hemoglobin 11.4 g/dL, and platelets 206 000 /µL. Venous lactate measured 1.9 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained before any hospital therapy revealed mild bilateral bibasilar infiltrates and elevated hemidiaphragms without pleural effusion, cardiomegaly, or pneumothorax. Twelve-lead electrocardiography performed during the arterial draw demonstrated normal sinus rhythm at 96 beats per minute, PR interval 180 ms, QRS 94 ms, and nonspecific lateral T-wave flattening but no acute ST-segment elevation or depression. Bedside focused cardiac ultrasound showed a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle with an inferior vena cava diameter of 1.4 cm that collapsed more than 50 % on inspiration, suggesting euvolemia rather than congestion. Bladder scan revealed 120 mL of urine, and he reported having voided shortly before the ambulance arrived. Importantly, during the thirty minutes between EMS arrival and acceptance by the critical-care team, he received no intravenous crystalloids, antibiotics, bronchodilators, diuretics, vasopressors, corticosteroids, or transfusions; thus the physiologic and laboratory data—temperature 98.5 °F, systolic pressure 140 mm Hg, diastolic pressure 80 mm Hg, heart rate 95 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, arterial pH 7.43, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.5 mmol/L, creatinine 1.3 mg/dL, hematocrit 34 %, white blood cell count 12 800 /mm³, fraction of inspired oxygen 38 %, and arterial oxygen tension 79 mm Hg—represent his untreated presentation for what is presumed to be early community-acquired pneumonia complicated by mild hypoxemia and transient confusion.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II adds acute physiology, age, and chronic health points. Using the supplied admission measurements:
- Temperature 98.5 °F (36.9 °C) → 0; mean arterial pressure = (140 + 2 × 80)/3 = 100 mmHg → 0.
- Heart rate 95/min → 0; respiratory rate 18/min → 0.
- FiO₂ is 0.38 (<0.50), so use PaO₂ rather than the alveolar–arterial gradient. PaO₂ 79 mmHg (>70) → 0.
- Arterial pH 7.43 → 0; sodium 138 mmol/L → 0; potassium 4.5 mmol/L → 0.
- Creatinine 1.3 mg/dL → 0; hematocrit 34% → 0; WBC 12.8 × 10³/µL → 0.
- Neurologic points = 15 − GCS = 15 − 14 = 1. Thus the acute physiology subtotal is 1.
Age 86 (≥75) → 6. No qualifying severe chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise → 0 chronic health points.
Total = 1 + 6 + 0 = 7.
Final answer: 7
